# Sedation Vacation in the ICU

**Authors:** Niraj K. Yadav, Joseph Maxwell Hendrix, Dominic J. Valentino III

**Source:** StatPearls - StatPearls Publishing

## Abstract

The intensive care unit (ICU) admits the hospital’s most critically ill and unstable patients who require accelerated and concentrated care. Approximately 33% of ICU admissions involve respiratory failure from various causes, with many patients requiring intubation and mechanical ventilatory support. Continuous sedation forms a key component of care for these patients, aiming to reduce pain and anxiety, decrease oxygen consumption and the body’s stress response, prevent patient-ventilator asynchrony, minimize adverse neurocognitive effects, eg, depression and posttraumatic stress disorder, reduce ventilator-associated complications, including pneumonia and tracheostomy, and facilitate nursing care. Mechanically ventilated patients often experience pain from endotracheal tubes, suctioning, indwelling catheters, surgical incisions, and frequent repositioning.  Sedation and analgesia are achieved using medications including benzodiazepines (eg, diazepam, lorazepam, and midazolam), opioid analgesics (eg, fentanyl, hydromorphone, morphine, and remifentanil), propofol, dexmedetomidine, ketamine, and antipsychotics (eg, haloperidol, quetiapine, and ziprasidone). No single agent has demonstrated superiority in efficacy or mortality benefit, though the Society of Critical Care Medicine recommends minimizing benzodiazepine use due to evidence of prolonged intubation. Sedative selection relies on clinical assessment, hemodynamic status, and a careful evaluation of risk-benefit profiles for each patient. Continuous sedation has been associated with longer intubation times, extended ICU stays, impaired neurological assessment, increased delirium, and suppressed EEG activity, correlating with higher 6-month mortality. Evidence supports daily, short-term cessation of sedation, or “sedation vacations,” to evaluate the ongoing need for sedation, titrate medications appropriately, and assess neurological status. Daily sedation interruptions reduce mechanical ventilation duration, ICU stay length, ventilator-associated infections, and the need for diagnostic tests related to oversedation. A study conducted in 80 patients revealed that a daily sedation vacation protocol in patients with intravenous sedation reduced the incidence of ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP); therefore, this protocol was recommended as a preventative measure for VAP. Furthermore, a randomized controlled trial in infants and children concluded that a sedation and ventilation weaning protocol significantly shortened the time to extubation compared to standard care.  Sedation vacations first emerged in 2000 through a study by J.P. Kress et al, establishing spontaneous-awakening trials as a standard ICU practice to facilitate ventilator weaning. The study of spontaneous-awakening trials showed that daily sedation interruptions improved the time to extubation of 64 patients by approximately 2 days, which reduced the total admission time in the ICU by 3.5 days. Subsequent trials, including the 2008 Awakening and Breathing Controlled trial (“Wake Up and Breathe” protocol) and the 2010 No Sedation in ICU Patients trial, reinforced these findings, demonstrating that structured protocols for sedation interruption and spontaneous breathing trials significantly reduce ventilator-dependent days and ICU admission duration compared to unstructured approaches or continuous sedation.
